newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -US ON BUY LIST VS BUNDS AFTER SELLOFF.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -US ON BUY LIST VS BUNDS AFTER SELLOFF.

text.p: Canny investors would do well to buy Treasuries against Bunds after Friday's shakeout in the U.S. market, economists said on Monday.
But they should tread carefully ahead of key U.S. retail sales data on Wednesday, particularly if the T-note/Bund spread heads back towards the sub 70 basis point level, they added.
"I would be a small scale buyer (of Treasuries) around these levels," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas in London.
"I wouldn't be too aggressive because the Treasury market is still fragile, but on a longer term view, this spread is attractive."
The Treasury market lost its footing on Friday as negative technicals, oversupply fears following the quarterly refunding, and nerves ahead of the July retail sales data took their toll.
European bond markets duly followed suit and took a tumble, though to a lesser extent on the whole, as Bunds found a slight momentum of their own.
The T-note/Bund spread snapped out 13 basis points on Friday and another three basis points on Monday, taking it to 77 basis points by 1055 GMT.
Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs, said that spread could temporarily dip below 70 basis points near term, before heading back out towards 90 to the year end.
"The selloff on Friday in the U.S. was a touch overdone, so I'd be inclined to think that spread might settle back to the sub 70 area," he said.
"We still have a bearish bias on Treasuries, but there's nothing immediately to hand that's likely to give the market further momentum at the moment, at least until we see the retail sales numbers."

McDevitt was more optimistic on the performance of Treasuries longer term. He saw the T-note/Bund spread going to 50 basis points in the next few months, then heading towards flat on a six to nine month view.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International Europe, also said the spread was on its way to 50 basis points to the year end.

"Near term, that spread will go to 70 basis points on its way to 50 longer term," he said. "The selloff has been overdone, but a resumption of the weak inflation, moderate growth story should entice investors back into the market," he said.
McDevitt said the key level to watch on the September T-bond future in the post-retail sales scramble was 112-00.
"I would definitely look for people to buy that (Treasury/Bund) spread now, but there is a risk, the key being that Treasuries hold above 112-00," he said.
July retail sales, due at 1230 GMT on Wednesday, are seen up 0.7 percent on the month, after rising 0.5 percent in June.
McDevitt and Bevan said that if the U.S. did take a hit on stronger than expected sales data, Treasuries would underperform their European counterparts.
"If Treasuries did break through 112-00, they would pull Europe down, but the latter would be much more resilient on the downside," said McDevitt.
"But also, if we get good data, Treasuries have more upside potential."
Bevan said it was tough to imagine the 10-year Bund yield breaking through 5.5 percent, particularly since the German curve had already priced in some interest rate tightening.
"So if Treasuries did rally, they could outperform on the upside," he said. By 1017 GMT, 10-year Bunds were yielding 5.7 percent.
